objects.why: A faint Milky Way satellite whose stars formed in several distinct bursts: a small galaxy with a stop-start history.

objects.name: Draco Dwarf
objects.why: One of the most dark-matter-dominated galaxies known: its stars move far too fast for the light we see.

objects.name: Ursa Minor Dwarf
objects.why: A near neighbour of the Milky Way whose stars are almost all ancient: it stopped forming them early.

objects.name: Sextans Dwarf
objects.why: So diffuse it was only found in 1990, on photographic plates scanned by machine.

objects.name: Leo I
objects.why: Sits in the glare of Regulus, one of the brightest stars in the sky, which hid it for decades.

objects.name: Leo II
objects.why: Leo I's fainter neighbour on the sky, a dwarf spheroidal found on the same 1950 survey plates.

objects.name: Barnard's Galaxy
objects.why: The first galaxy beyond the Magellanic Clouds to have its distance measured, by Hubble in 1925, from its Cepheid stars.

objects.name: IC 10
objects.why: The Local Group's only starburst galaxy, seen dimly through the dust of the Milky Way's own disc.

objects.name: IC 1613
objects.why: A quiet irregular dwarf so free of dust that it anchors the Cepheid distance scale.

objects.name: Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte
objects.why: An isolated dwarf at the edge of the Local Group that has lived its whole life alone.

objects.name: Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal
objects.why: On the far side of the Milky Way's centre and being torn apart by it: its stars now trail right round our galaxy in a stream.

objects.name: NGC 147
objects.why: A satellite of Andromeda, paired on the sky with NGC 185, and a bridge of stars runs between the two.

objects.name: NGC 185
objects.why: Andromeda's satellite with a faint active nucleus: the nearest Seyfert galaxy, and a dwarf at that.

objects.name: Sextans A
objects.why: A square-looking dwarf at the very edge of the Local Group, its shape carved by supernova blasts.

objects.name: Sextans B
objects.why: Sextans A's neighbour, one of the most distant members still counted in the Local Group.

objects.name: Leo A
objects.why: An isolated dwarf that made most of its stars late, long after the rest of the Local Group had settled down.

objects.name: Pegasus Dwarf Irregular
objects.typeText: transition dwarf galaxy, part irregular, part spheroidal
objects.why: A distant companion of Andromeda caught between two kinds: still a little gas, hardly any new stars.

objects.name: Phoenix Dwarf
objects.why: Found in 1976 and taken for a globular cluster at first; a small galaxy with a cloud of gas drifting away from it.

objects.name: Tucana Dwarf
objects.why: A lonely dwarf on the opposite side of the Local Group from Andromeda, far from any big galaxy.

objects.name: Cetus Dwarf
objects.why: An isolated spheroidal dwarf found in 1999; most of its kind cling to a big galaxy, this one does not.

objects.name: Aquarius Dwarf
objects.why: A faint irregular dwarf so isolated that it is used to test how galaxies grow with nothing disturbing them.

objects.name: Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular
objects.why: Not the Sagittarius Dwarf being eaten by the Milky Way: a separate, far more distant irregular dwarf in the same constellation.

objects.name: Antlia Dwarf
objects.why: Found only in 1997, a companion of NGC 3109 at the Local Group's edge, proof that the neighbourhood still has galaxies to find.

objects.name: Andromeda II
objects.why: One of Andromeda's small spheroidal companions, found in 1970 on photographic plates.

objects.name: Andromeda I
objects.why: The first of Andromeda's small spheroidal companions to be numbered, found by Sidney van den Bergh in 1970.

objects.name: Andromeda III
objects.why: Another of Andromeda's faint companions from the 1970 plates, a little farther out than the first.

objects.name: NGC 3109
objects.why: A thin edge-on streak at the Local Group's outer edge; whether it belongs to the Group at all is still argued.

objects.name: Ursa Major II Dwarf
objects.why: One of the ultra-faint dwarfs found in Sloan survey data in 2006: a few thousand stars, spread over a patch the size of the full Moon.

objects.name: Segue 1
objects.typeText: ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, or perhaps a star cluster
objects.why: Among the faintest galaxies known, a few hundred stars held together by far more dark matter than light, if it is a galaxy at all.

objects.name: Leo T
objects.typeText: transition dwarf galaxy, part spheroidal, part irregular
objects.why: The faintest galaxy known to still hold gas and make the odd new star, found in Sloan survey data in 2007.

objects.name: Bootes I
objects.why: One of the faintest galaxies known when it was found in 2006; a few hundred thousand stars where a normal galaxy has billions.

objects.name: Canes Venatici I
objects.why: A remote Milky Way satellite with two separate generations of stars, found in 2006.

objects.name: Ursa Major I Dwarf
objects.why: Found in 2005, the first of the ultra-faint dwarfs the Sloan survey turned up around the Milky Way.

objects.name: Reticulum II
objects.why: Found in 2015 in Dark Energy Survey data; its stars are rich in the heavy elements a merger of two neutron stars makes.

objects.name: Leo IV
objects.why: A faint Sloan-survey dwarf with a neighbour, Leo V, close enough on the sky that the two may be linked.

objects.name: Willman 1
objects.why: Named for Beth Willman, who found it in 2005: for years nobody was sure whether it was a galaxy or a star cluster.

objects.name: Pisces II
objects.why: A faint satellite found in 2010, one of the most distant of the Milky Way's dwarfs.

objects.name: Sculptor Galaxy
objects.typeText: spiral galaxy, seen nearly edge-on and bursting with new stars
objects.why: One of the brightest galaxies beyond the Local Group, a dusty starburst spiral tilted almost edge-on to us.

objects.name: Centaurus A
objects.typeText: peculiar galaxy with a giant black hole firing radio jets
objects.why: The nearest galaxy with jets: a dark dust lane across a round glow, and radio lobes many times its size, from a black hole eating a swallowed spiral.

objects.why: The second-brightest globular cluster, a naked-eye ball of stars next to the Small Magellanic Cloud, though about 190 000 light-years nearer.

objects.name: Carina Nebula
objects.distanceSource: Smith 2006, ApJ 644, 1151; Göppl & Preibisch 2022, A&A 660, A11 (arXiv:2201.09097)
objects.why: Four times the size of the Orion Nebula and brighter, home to Eta Carinae and some of the heaviest stars known; the south's great nebula.

distance.source: Smith 2006, ApJ 644, 1151; Göppl & Preibisch 2022, A&A 660, A11 (arXiv:2201.09097)

objects.name: Helix Nebula
objects.distanceSource: Gaia DR2 parallax of the central star (VizieR I/345), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix_Nebula
objects.why: One of the nearest planetary nebulae, the shell a dying Sun-like star has thrown off; the 'Eye of God' photographs.

distance.source: Gaia DR2 parallax of the central star (VizieR I/345), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix_Nebula

objects.name: Cat's Eye Nebula
objects.why: The first planetary nebula whose light was split into a spectrum (1864), showing glowing gas, not stars; Hubble's portrait of it is famous.

objects.name: Double Cluster
objects.why: Two young star clusters side by side in binoculars, born together about 13 million years ago.

objects.name: Hyades
objects.why: The nearest open cluster, the V of stars that makes the Bull's face; Aldebaran sits in front of it but is not a member.

objects.name: Rosette Nebula
objects.why: A ring of glowing gas round a young cluster whose stars have blown the middle clear: a rose with a hollow heart.

objects.name: North America Nebula
objects.why: Shaped like the continent, with a dark 'Gulf of Mexico' of dust; a naked-eye glow from a truly dark site.

objects.name: NGC 891
objects.why: What the Milky Way would look like from outside and exactly edge-on: a thin disc split by a dark lane of dust.

objects.name: Jewel Box
objects.why: A small cluster of blue-white stars with one red supergiant among them: Herschel's 'casket of variously coloured precious stones'.

objects.name: Tarantula Nebula
objects.distanceSource: its parent's (Large Magellanic Cloud): Pietrzyński et al. 2019, Nature 567, 200 (arXiv:1903.08096)
objects.positionSource: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarantula_Nebula (infobox, read 2026-09-09); placed where its line of sight meets the plane of Large Magellanic Cloud's disc (van der Marel & Cioni 2001, AJ 122, 1807 (arXiv:astro-ph/0105339))
objects.why: The most violent star factory in the Local Group, in another galaxy: put where the Orion Nebula is, it would cast shadows.

distance.source: parent

objects.name: Veil Nebula
objects.why: The torn shell of a star that exploded ten to twenty thousand years ago, six full Moons across, in lacework filaments.

objects.name: Coalsack Nebula
objects.why: A hole in the Milky Way next to the Southern Cross: not a hole but a cloud of dust so thick no starlight gets through.

objects.name: Bubble Nebula
objects.why: A hot giant star blowing a bubble ten light-years wide into the cloud that made it.

objects.name: Intergalactic Wanderer

objects.why: A globular cluster farther out than the Magellanic Clouds, once thought to be leaving the galaxy. It is not leaving; it takes three billion years to go round.

objects.name: Eskimo Nebula
objects.why: A face in a fur hood: a dying star's shell seen down its axis, with a ring of comet-like streamers round it.

objects.name: Saturn Nebula
objects.why: Two jets stick out of its sides like Saturn's rings seen edge-on, which is how it got its name in 1840.

objects.name: NGC 7331
objects.why: Once called the Milky Way's twin: a big spiral seen at a tilt, with a bulge that turns the opposite way to its disc.

objects.name: Satellite Cluster
objects.why: The young stars in the heart of the Rosette Nebula; their light is what makes the rose glow.

objects.name: Wishing Well Cluster
objects.why: Hundreds of stars like coins at the bottom of a well; the first target the Hubble Space Telescope ever pointed at, in 1990.

objects.name: Southern Pleiades
objects.why: The south's answer to the Pleiades, round the star Theta Carinae: a naked-eye cluster the north never sees.

objects.name: NGC 6231
objects.why: A tight knot of hot young stars in the Scorpion's tail, the core of a much larger stellar association.

objects.name: Flame Nebula
objects.why: Next to Alnitak in Orion's Belt, a glowing cloud split by a dark lane of dust, with a cluster of newborn stars hidden inside.

objects.name: Horsehead Nebula
objects.why: The most famous dark cloud in the sky: a horse's head of dust against the red glow of IC 434, below Orion's Belt.

objects.name: Thor's Helmet
objects.why: A bubble blown by WR 7, an extremely hot star thought to be close to going supernova; a nearby gas cloud gave it its curved, complex shape.

objects.name: Butterfly Nebula
objects.why: Its central white dwarf, one of the hottest stars known at over 250 000 °C, hides behind a dark lane of dust across the waist of its two lobes.

objects.name: Ghost of Jupiter
objects.why: Named for its likeness to Jupiter in a telescope: a bluish-green disc about two light-years long, its inner layers thrown off some 1 500 years ago.

objects.name: Blue Snowball Nebula
objects.why: A small bluish disc in a modest telescope: shells of gas a dying star threw off about 3 000 years ago, lit by a core of about 100 000 degrees.

objects.name: Skull Nebula
objects.why: The first planetary nebula known to have three stars at its centre: a white dwarf and two companions, the third found in 2014.

objects.name: Christmas Tree Cluster
objects.typeText: young open cluster in an emission nebula
objects.why: A young cluster shaped like an upside-down Christmas tree, with the Cone Nebula at its tip; new stars are still forming in its dust.

objects.name: Heart Nebula
objects.why: Hydrogen glowing red in the light of a young cluster at its centre, whose brightest stars are nearly 50 times the mass of the Sun.

objects.name: Soul Nebula
objects.why: The Heart Nebula's eastern neighbour: its stars get younger the farther they sit from the hollows its biggest stars blew, as if each generation lit the next.

objects.name: Iris Nebula
objects.why: Dust lit by a young double star; buckyballs, football-shaped molecules of 60 carbon atoms, were first firmly found in interstellar space here and in NGC 2023.

objects.name: Cocoon Nebula
objects.why: A star nursery at the head of a long dark trail of dust, Barnard 168; Spitzer and Chandra found hundreds of young stars in it.

objects.name: Cat's Paw Nebula
objects.why: Round glowing pads like a cat's paw, with ten star clusters hidden in its dust; in 2025 Webb looked inside one 'toe bean' and saw stars forming.

objects.name: War and Peace Nebula
objects.why: Home to the cluster Pismis 24, whose brightest star was once thought to weigh 300 Suns, until it turned out to be at least three stars.

objects.name: Needle Galaxy
objects.why: A giant spiral more luminous than Andromeda, seen edge-on as a thin needle of light; the edge of its disc is slightly warped.

objects.name: Whale Galaxy
objects.why: An edge-on spiral shaped like a whale or a herring, where so many stars have exploded that their wind blows gas out of the galaxy's disc.

objects.name: NGC 2403
objects.why: The first galaxy beyond the Local Group in which a Cepheid variable star was found, by Edwin Hubble; an outlying member of the M81 group.

objects.name: Fireworks Galaxy
objects.why: Ten supernovae seen between 1917 and 2017, about ten times the Milky Way's rate from a galaxy with half as many stars: hence the Fireworks.

objects.name: NGC 55
objects.typeText: barred spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on
objects.why: Seen nearly edge-on, like a smaller Large Magellanic Cloud; it and NGC 300 lie in front of the Sculptor Group and are likely a bound pair.

objects.name: NGC 300
objects.why: A spiral much like the Triangulum Galaxy; its distance, 6.07 million light-years, comes from Cepheid stars and red giants, two methods that agree.

objects.name: NGC 1300
objects.why: A barred spiral with a second, grand-design spiral 3 300 light-years long in its core: a spiral within a spiral, seen only in galaxies with big bars.

objects.name: Antennae Galaxies
objects.why: Two galaxies in collision, flinging out two long tails of stars and gas like an insect's antennae; the crash is setting off bursts of new stars.

objects.name: Blinking Planetary
objects.why: Stare at it and the bright central star drowns the nebula; look aside and the nebula comes back, so it seems to blink on and off.

objects.name: Wizard Nebula
objects.typeText: young open cluster in an emission nebula
objects.why: A young cluster found by Caroline Herschel in 1787; the pair of massive stars at its centre lights the Wizard Nebula and drives its gas outward.

objects.name: Pacman Nebula
objects.why: Shaped like the video-game Pac-Man: glowing gas round the young cluster IC 1590, with small dark globules of dust against it.

objects.name: Crescent Nebula
objects.why: The fast wind of the Wolf-Rayet star WR 136 slamming into the slower wind it shed as a red giant some 250 000 years ago.

objects.name: Hamburger Galaxy
objects.why: The third galaxy of the Leo Triplet, with M65 and M66: a band of dust splits it like a hamburger, and a tidal tail 300 000 light-years long streams away.

objects.name: California Nebula
objects.why: Shaped like the state of California, and by coincidence it passes straight overhead in central California, whose latitude matches its declination.

objects.name: Southern Ring Nebula
objects.why: One of the five targets of the Webb telescope's first science images, July 2022: a dying star's shells, with a white dwarf and a companion at the centre.

objects.name: NGC 7027
objects.why: A planetary nebula in the earliest stage of its life, about 600 years old, and one of the smallest known: 0.2 light-years long where most are one.

objects.name: Owl Cluster
objects.why: Two bright stars make the eyes of an owl, or of E.T.; if the brighter, Phi Cassiopeiae, truly belongs to the cluster, it outshines Rigel.

objects.name: Caroline's Rose
objects.why: Found by Caroline Herschel in 1783: loops of stars and dark lanes like the petals of a rose seen from above, 1.4 to 1.7 billion years old.
